source.title: n8n 2.43.5: eager VM expression-isolate acquisition adds alternating latency to minimal production webhooks

source.body:
### Bug Description

On self-hosted n8n 2.43.5, production webhook executions exhibit recurring latency spikes even with a minimal two-node workflow (`Webhook → Respond to Webhook`).

Sequential HTTP requests sent directly to `127.0.0.1:5678` reproduce alternating fast (~50–70 ms) and slow (~210–300 ms) response times. This excludes external reverse-proxy and TLS overhead from the reproduction path.

We instrumented the installed execution engine and identified the recurring delay in:

`WorkflowExecute.initializeExecution() → workflow.expression.acquireIsolate()`

Across the diagnostic executions, isolate acquisition took approximately 5–7 ms on fast runs and 168–186 ms on slow runs. The workflow nodes themselves executed quickly.

Source inspection showed that `ExpressionEvaluator.acquire()` obtains an initialized bridge from `IsolatePool`, but falls back to asynchronous `createBridge()` if the pool is exhausted. The pool replenishes bridges asynchronously and disposes acquired bridges on release.

This suggests that pool exhaustion and cold bridge initialization may explain the observed latency pattern. However, per-request pool availability and cold-start events were not directly instrumented, so this remains a hypothesis rather than a proven root cause.

**Observed mitigation:**

Enabling `N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_LAZY_ACQUIRE=true`, together with pool size 2, substantially improved the minimal workflow's steady-state response times.

After the first two post-restart requests (3252 ms and 377 ms), the following 18 requests completed in approximately 51–80 ms, with no recurring >200 ms spike in that sample.

Real application workflows also completed successfully during subsequent Stage smoke tests, including dynamic-expression evaluation and authenticated application navigation.

We are reporting this because an otherwise minimal webhook appears to incur significant VM expression-isolate initialization overhead even when no dynamic expression evaluation is required.

### To Reproduce

Deploy the official Docker image docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n:2.43.5 with the default VM expression-engine configuration:

N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE=vm

N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_POOL_SIZE=1

N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_LAZY_ACQUIRE=false

These are the installed defaults; explicit environment variables are not required.

Create and activate a minimal workflow:

Webhook node using HTTP GET and a static path.

Respond to Webhook node returning a simple static response.

Configure the Webhook node to use the Respond to Webhook node for its response.

Do not add dynamic expressions or Code nodes.

Send 20 sequential requests directly to the n8n instance:

for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  curl -sS -o /dev/null \
    -w "Request $i | HTTP %{http_code} | %{time_total}s\n" \
    http://127.0.0.1:5678/webhook/isolated/test
done

Observe recurring slow responses interspersed with fast responses.

Repeat with N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_POOL_SIZE=2 and N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_LAZY_ACQUIRE=false. Slow requests become less frequent but remain present.

Repeat with:

N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_POOL_SIZE=2

N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_LAZY_ACQUIRE=true

Restart the test instance, allow startup to finish, and repeat the benchmark. In our environment, steady-state latency spikes disappeared from the 18 requests following the initial two warm-up requests.

Measured results:

Configuration

Results

Pool 1, eager

Alternating ~50–70 ms / ~210–300 ms

Pool 2, eager, run 1

6/20 requests >200 ms; maximum 573 ms

Pool 2, eager, run 2

3/20 requests >200 ms; maximum 459 ms

Pool 2, lazy

First two requests 3252/377 ms; remaining 18 ~51–80 ms, 0/18 >200 ms

No external HTTP proxy was involved in the direct localhost benchmark.

### Expected behavior

A production webhook workflow that does not evaluate dynamic expressions should not incur significant recurring VM isolate initialization overhead.

After application initialization, repeated requests to an otherwise minimal workflow should show relatively consistent response times without regularly adding approximately 170–185 ms during `acquireIsolate()`.

If eager isolate acquisition is intentional, it would be helpful to clarify the expected latency characteristics, pool replenishment behaviour, and recommended production configuration for simple webhook workloads.

### Debug Info

Environment

n8n version: 2.43.5

Deployment: Self-hosted Docker Compose, official n8n image

Expression engine: VM (isolated-vm bridge)

Default expression pool size: 1

Default lazy acquisition: false

Execution mode: regular

PostgreSQL: 16.2

External JavaScript and Python task runners enabled

Host resources: approximately 1.9 GiB RAM and 2 GiB swap

Test route: local HTTP directly to port 5678

Instrumentation findings

We instrumented the installed n8n execution engine at workflow initialization and surrounding execution phases.

Example consecutive isolate-acquisition durations (ms):

Execution A:   5.156
Execution B: 182.627
Execution C:   5.778
Execution D: 182.852
Execution E:   5.198
Execution F: 186.227
Execution G:   6.416
Execution H: 180.081

The delay occurs in:

WorkflowExecute.initializeExecution()
  → workflow.expression.acquireIsolate()
    → Expression.vmEvaluator.acquire(this)

Relevant installed implementation files:

n8n-core/dist/execution-engine/workflow-execute.js
n8n-workflow/dist/cjs/expression.js
@n8n/expression-runtime/dist/cjs/evaluator/expression-evaluator.js
@n8n/expression-runtime/dist/cjs/pool/isolate-pool.js

ExpressionEvaluator.acquire() handles PoolExhaustedError by calling await this.createBridge(). IsolatePool.acquire() removes an initialized bridge and initiates asynchronous replenishment.

Additional observations

Localhost reproduction removes external proxy/TLS from the measured path.

Disabling execution-data saving did not eliminate the latency pattern.

The pattern was reproduced using a minimal two-node workflow.

Increasing pool size partially improved results.

Lazy acquisition substantially improved steady-state minimal-webhook latency.

Basic dynamic expressions and real application navigation passed Stage smoke tests.

Pool exhaustion/cold creation is a suspected explanation, not directly proven by pool-state instrumentation.

No equivalent controlled benchmark on n8n 1.x was recorded.

Questions for maintainers

Is the observed eager isolate acquisition expected for workflows containing no dynamic expressions?

Is there a reason N8N_EXPRESSION_ENGINE_LAZY_ACQUIRE defaults to false?

Is per-execution isolate disposal and asynchronous replacement the intended pool lifecycle?

Are there known trade-offs or compatibility limitations when enabling lazy acquisition for production workflows?

Would upstream instrumentation of pool exhaustion and cold-start durations be useful for diagnosing this behaviour?

We can provide additional redacted timing logs and a minimal workflow export if requested.

### Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04.1 LTS

### n8n Version

2.43.5

### Node.js Version

v26.7.0

### Database

PostgreSQL

### Execution mode

main (default)

### Hosting

self hosted

comments.author: ardaerturk
comments.text:
One instrumentation distinction in the **2.43.5 source** may help with the next benchmark: the existing synchronous cold-start metric cannot confirm or rule out the eager-path cold starts in this report.

- [`initializeExecution()` acquires an isolate before running the workflow](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/d811f5e87dfc164999f34d75b17017876d41a54a/packages/core/src/execution-engine/workflow-execute.ts#L1678-L1694). In [`ExpressionEvaluator.acquire()`](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/d811f5e87dfc164999f34d75b17017876d41a54a/packages/%40n8n/expression-runtime/src/evaluator/expression-evaluator.ts#L119-L139), eager mode takes a warm bridge or awaits `createBridge()` after `PoolExhaustedError`. Lazy mode opens a scope without taking a bridge. This explains why the static two-node case can benefit without establishing the cause of the alternating timings.
- [`IsolatePool.acquire()` starts asynchronous replenishment; `release()` disposes the used bridge](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/d811f5e87dfc164999f34d75b17017876d41a54a/packages/%40n8n/expression-runtime/src/pool/isolate-pool.ts#L63-L78). The used bridge is not returned as a reusable warm entry.
- [`expression.pool.cold_start_sync` and its duration metric](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/d811f5e87dfc164999f34d75b17017876d41a54a/packages/%40n8n/expression-runtime/src/evaluator/expression-evaluator.ts#L141-L179) cover the **lazy, synchronous** fallback. The eager fallback above has no corresponding cold-start counter at that call site; both warm and cold eager acquisitions increment `poolAcquired`. Also, the evaluation-duration timer starts after `getBridge()`, so that timer excludes bridge acquisition.

For the existing Stage reproduction, I would keep the image, pool size and request spacing fixed, then compare eager/lazy on (1) the static response and (2) an otherwise identical response that evaluates one dynamic expression. Record the acquisition path (`warm` or `cold`), acquisition milliseconds, total request milliseconds, HTTP status and whether the expected response was correct. Keep the same predeclared warm-up rule in each run and retain the cold-start results separately. A short idle gap between requests is another useful, separate comparison for the replenishment hypothesis.

The trade-off to check is explicit in the [configuration comment](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/d811f5e87dfc164999f34d75b17017876d41a54a/packages/%40n8n/config/src/configs/expression-engine.config.ts#L97-L105): lazy acquisition is marked experimental, and an empty pool can make the first engine evaluation build its isolate synchronously on the request path. The static case avoids that work; expression-bearing workloads can still pay it. This source reading does not establish why the default was chosen or certify production compatibility.

I operate Keptick with AI assistance. This is a review of the tagged source, not an independent Docker reproduction or a rerun of its tests. A redacted timing table containing those fields would help distinguish pool misses from another source of delay; workflow payloads and credentials are unnecessary.
